definition: An electronic instrument, in hardware or software, that creates and shapes audio from control information. Its sound engine may generate waveforms, combine sine components, process recorded samples or simulate vibrating objects; filters, envelopes and modulation shape the result.
example: A monophonic subtractive synthesiser can be built from one oscillator, one filter, one amplifier, two envelopes and an LFO.

definition: Varying an oscillator’s instantaneous frequency with another signal. Slow changes can give vibrato; audio-rate sinusoidal modulation of a sine carrier creates sidebands on a grid spaced by the modulator frequency. Their amplitudes depend on the modulation index.
example: A 100 Hz modulator on a 400 Hz carrier creates sidebands at 300, 500, 200, 600 Hz and so on.

definition: Varying an oscillator's phase, rather than its frequency, with another signal. It is mathematically closely related to FM: phase-modulating with a signal is equivalent to frequency-modulating with that signal’s rate of change, with the appropriate conversion between phase and frequency units. Yamaha's "FM" synths, including the DX7, are implemented as phase modulation.
example: In PM a modulator with a constant (DC) offset only shifts the carrier's phase, whereas in true FM it would shift its pitch.

definition: The two roles in FM or PM synthesis. The carrier is the oscillator you hear; the modulator is the oscillator that varies the carrier's frequency or phase. Their frequency ratio decides where the sidebands fall, and so whether the result sounds harmonic or bell-like.
example: A 400 Hz sine carrier and 100 Hz sinusoidal modulator produce possible sideband positions on a 100 Hz grid. More complicated ratios can give metallic timbres; particular components can cancel or vanish.

definition: A frequency component created by modulation, at an offset from a carrier. For constant-depth sinusoidal linear FM or PM of a sine carrier, possible components lie on a grid spaced by the modulator frequency. Their amplitudes depend on modulation index, and coincident components can add or cancel.
example: A 440 Hz carrier modulated at 110 Hz has its first pair of sidebands at 330 Hz and 550 Hz.

definition: For sinusoidal linear FM, the peak frequency deviation divided by the modulator frequency, a dimensionless measure of modulation depth. In the equivalent sinusoidal PM expression it is the peak phase deviation in radians. A low non-zero index concentrates energy in the carrier and first sideband pairs; a higher index generally distributes significant energy across more pairs, with individual Bessel-function zeros.
example: Sweeping the modulation index with an envelope makes an FM sound start bright and then mellow, like a struck bell.

definition: Yamaha’s digital synthesiser introduced in 1983, built around a six-operator FM sound engine. Its carrier/modulator algorithms made complex spectra and evolving timbres possible with a small number of oscillators; it is an important historical example of musical FM/PM.

aliases: Center for Computer Research in Music and Acoustics
definition: Stanford University’s Center for Computer Research in Music and Acoustics, where musicians and researchers study computer-based sound and music. Julius O. Smith publishes authoritative DSP textbooks there; its researchers have published work on synthesis, physical models and digital filters.

One period of a waveform stored as a short array of samples. A phase accumulator repeatedly reads it to make a tone. The usable pitch range depends on its harmonics, interpolation and sample rate; storing a cycle does not automatically prevent aliasing.
example: A 2,048-sample table holding one cycle of a sawtooth can be played at 100 Hz or 1 kHz just by changing the phase increment.

definition: The German company founded by Wolfgang Palm whose Wave synthesisers (from the early 1980s) popularised wavetable synthesis, stepping through sets of stored single-cycle waveforms.
A German synthesiser maker whose instruments continued Wolfgang Palm's wavetable approach after PPG closed, starting with the Microwave in 1989.

Making notes by playing back recordings (samples) of real sounds, re-pitched by reading them faster or slower, then shaping them with envelopes and filters. It sounds realistic but uses a lot of memory, and its expression is limited to what was recorded.
example: Reading a recording at twice its original speed raises its pitch by an octave and halves its length.

definition: A synthesis method that simulates the physics of a sound source, such as a vibrating string, an air column or a drum membrane, instead of describing the waveform directly. Model parameters (stiffness, damping, size) control the sound.
example: Karplus–Strong is the classic small example: a delay line and a filter imitate a plucked string.

definition: A simple physical-modelling algorithm for plucked strings: fill a short delay line with noise and feed it back through a gentle low-pass (averaging) filter. The loop length sets the pitch, and the filter makes high harmonics die away first, as on a real string.
example: At 48 kHz, a loop of about 218 samples gives a pitch of about 220 Hz.

definition: An analogue monophonic synthesiser made by Moog Music from 1970, with three oscillators, Moog's 24 dB/octave ladder low-pass filter and envelope generators. Its compact oscillator–filter–amplifier layout became the template for subtractive synths.
An oscillator whose frequency is set by a control voltage. In analogue synths the VCO is the sound source; the name is often kept for the oscillator block in digital synths too.
example: In many analogue synths raising a VCO's control voltage by 1 V raises its pitch by one octave (the "volt per octave" convention).

definition: An analogue sound-producing oscillator whose cycle timing is set by a digital clock or counter. Digital timing can stabilise tuning, while the waveform path remains analogue; it is distinct from computing every output sample in a wholly digital oscillator.
A filter whose cutoff (and often resonance) is set by a control voltage, so envelopes and LFOs can sweep it. In a synth voice it is usually a resonant low-pass.
The second stage of an ADSR envelope: the fall from the peak to the sustain level while the key is still held.
example: With sustain at 0 and a 300 ms decay, a held note dies away like a pluck.

definition: The third ADSR control, and the only one that is a level rather than a time: the value the envelope holds for as long as the key stays down, after attack and decay have finished.
example: Sustain 0.6 holds the note at 60% of the envelope's peak until the key is released.

definition: A second envelope, scaled by an amount, that is added to the filter cutoff so the sound's brightness changes over each note. Short attack and decay with low sustain give the classic pluck or "squelch".
example: A filter envelope amount of 3 octaves takes a 500 Hz cutoff up to 4 kHz at the envelope's peak.

definition: A periodic variation in loudness, usually produced by an LFO routed to the amplifier's gain. (Some instruments and effects use the words tremolo and vibrato loosely; synths use them precisely.)
example: A 6 Hz tremolo with depth 0.5 takes the volume down to half and back six times a second.

definition: A signal carrying the intended sound through an audio path, such as oscillator, filter, amplifier and output. A digital audio signal is a stream of samples; an analogue signal varies continuously. Its role distinguishes it from a parameter-control signal.

A signal that steers something else rather than being the main data or sound itself. In a synth, control signals are envelopes, LFOs, knob positions and MIDI values that set parameters; they usually change slowly and can often be computed less often than audio. (In a CPU, the control unit's control signals similarly tell the datapath what to do.)
example: A 5 Hz LFO routed to pitch is a control signal; the oscillator output it modulates is an audio signal.

definition: The number of audio blocks processed each second: the sample rate divided by samples per block. A parameter updated once per block has this update opportunity rate. Resetting an otherwise identical waveform at every block makes a repeating block, whose spectrum lies on multiples of that rate.
example: At 48 kHz with 64-sample blocks, there are 750 blocks per second.

definition: A synth architecture that can play several pitches while sharing part of the sound-shaping path, commonly a filter and its envelope. Shared shaping affects held notes together; exact amplifier and triggering arrangements vary by instrument.
example: In a paraphonic design that retriggers its shared filter envelope on each new key, adding a note also sweeps the held notes.

definition: The position in an oscillator’s cycle, often stored as a wrapped fraction from 0 up to 1. An unwrapped phase measured in cycles also counts completed turns. Preserve the chosen phase state across samples and audio blocks so a frequency change does not restart the waveform.
example: A phase of 0.25 means a quarter of the way through the cycle, where a sine is at its peak.

definition: The unit of a phase increment: what fraction of a waveform cycle passes during one sample. Its reciprocal, samples per cycle, is the length of one period in samples.
example: At 48 kHz, a 440 Hz tone advances 0.0091667 cycles per sample, so one cycle lasts about 109 samples.

definition: Running continuously without being reset. A free-running oscillator's phase is never reset on a new note, so each note starts at whatever point in the cycle the oscillator has reached, giving slight note-to-note variation, as on many analogue synths.

Setting an oscillator’s phase to a chosen start point, often at note-on. This makes the waveform start reproducibly. Resetting while a voice is audible can cause a discontinuity and click, so the envelope or fade policy matters.

Frequency modulation deep enough to drive the oscillator's instantaneous frequency below zero, so its phase runs backwards for a while. The phase-wrapping code must then handle negative phases as well as phases above 1.
The function that rounds a number up to the nearest whole number, written ⌈x⌉, so ⌈43.64⌉ = 44 and ⌈7⌉ = 7.
example: Resetting phase to zero makes each 1100 Hz cycle at 48 kHz last ⌈43.64⌉ = 44 samples.

definition: The C library function that returns the floating-point remainder of a division. Its result takes the sign of the first argument, so fmod(−0.3, 1.0) is −0.3, which makes it the wrong tool for wrapping a phase that can go negative.
A technique, and a family of chips, that generate precise, finely tunable waveforms with a numerically controlled oscillator feeding a digital-to-analogue converter.

The optional exact-width unsigned 32-bit integer type in C and C++, when the implementation provides it. It represents zero through 4,294,967,295. Storing the result of the illustrated unsigned phase addition back into this type gives modulo-two-to-the-thirty-two wrapping; signed integer overflow has different rules.
example: 4,294,967,295 + 1 wraps to 0 in a uint32_t.

definition: Moving bits left or right within an integer representation. For a non-negative unsigned value, a valid right shift discards low bits and is equivalent to integer division by the corresponding power of two. An integer oscillator uses this to obtain the high phase bits for a table index.
example: Shifting a 32-bit phase right by 21 keeps its top 11 bits, an index from 0 to 2,047.

definition: An array of precomputed values that replaces a calculation with an index operation. In synths it typically holds one cycle of a waveform, read at a position set by the oscillator's phase.
example: A 2,048-entry sine table lets an oscillator fetch a sine value instead of calling sin().

definition: Any single sine-wave component of a sound, whether or not it is a whole-number multiple of the fundamental. Additive synthesis sets the level of each partial directly.
The representation of a periodic waveform as its average (DC) value plus a sum of sine waves at whole-number multiples of its fundamental, each with its own amplitude and phase.
example: A ±1 square wave is (4/π) times the sum of sin(nωt)/n over odd n.

definition: Ripple and overshoot near a jump when a Fourier series is limited to finitely many terms. As the term count grows, the overshoot approaches about 8.95% of the jump size while its region narrows. A hard-truncated ideal square with levels plus and minus one therefore approaches peaks near plus and minus 1.179; other smoothing kernels can change this.
Whistling tones caused by aliasing that slide in the wrong direction (or erratically) when a naive oscillator's pitch is swept, because folded harmonics can move down as the note goes up.

Several precomputed versions of a waveform table, typically one per octave, each containing only the harmonics that stay below Nyquist for the highest note it will play. The oscillator picks the table for the current pitch. The name comes from mipmapping in computer graphics.
example: At 48 kHz, a table for notes up to 2 kHz may hold 11 harmonics; one for notes up to 1 kHz may hold 23.

definition: A signal made of single spikes repeating at a fixed interval. Its spectrum contains every harmonic at equal strength, and integrating it (once its average value is removed) gives a sawtooth.

A process that keeps a running total of its input; digitally it adds each new sample to the previous output. Integrating a zero-average impulse train gives a sawtooth, and integrating a square wave gives a triangle.

A running sum with feedback slightly below unity, so old contributions decay rather than accumulating indefinitely. With finite input and a valid stable coefficient it cannot build up unboundedly from a fixed DC offset, although its DC gain can be large. DaisySP’s checked triangle oscillator integrates a corrected square this way.
example: DaisySP makes its PolyBLEP triangle by passing a PolyBLEP square through a leaky integrator.

definition: Eli Brandt's 2001 BLEP method: precompute a band-limited step, make it minimum-phase, and store its difference from an ideal step in a table. At each jump the oscillator adds the table, aligned to the jump's exact fractional position.
The equivalent of a BLEP for corners (sudden changes of slope) rather than jumps, used to band-limit triangle waves and other waveforms with sharp corners.

A causal stable filter or correction kernel whose phase is minimum among causal stable responses with the same magnitude response, under the usual minimum-phase conditions. Its energy is concentrated early compared with other phase choices. Brandt’s minBLEP uses this to put the correction after the edge without lookahead; minimum phase does not mean no ringing.

An expression built by multiplying non-negative whole-number powers of variables by constants and adding the terms, such as 2u − u² − 1. A small fixed-degree polynomial is cheap to evaluate, which is why the shown PolyBLEP uses one instead of a correction table.

Estimating a value between two known points by drawing a straight line between them. Wavetable oscillators use it to read between table entries, and control-rate code uses it to spread a new value smoothly across a block.
example: Halfway between table values 0.2 and 0.6, linear interpolation gives 0.4.

definition: Two envelope behaviours on a mono synth. Multi-trigger restarts the envelopes on every new note; single-trigger (legato) only restarts them when a key is pressed with no other key held, so overlapping notes change pitch without a new attack.
A widely used C++ framework for building audio applications and plug-ins. Its SmoothedValue class provides linear and multiplicative parameter smoothing.

A JUCE utility that ramps values towards a target over a chosen number of samples, linearly or by equal multiplicative ratios. Equal ratios suit pitch and decibel-style changes. Multiplicative smoothing cannot reach a target of zero, so silence needs another policy.
Short for band-pass: a filter that passes a band of frequencies around its centre and reduces those on both sides.

How a filter’s magnitude changes as frequency changes, often expressed in decibels per octave. For an analogue-style all-pole low-pass far into the stopband, each pole contributes about 6 dB per octave. Zeros and digital behaviour near Nyquist can change that rule.
example: A 24 dB/oct low-pass at 500 Hz cuts a 4 kHz harmonic by roughly 72 dB.

definition: A root of a transfer function’s denominator after pole-zero cancellations, representing part of the filter’s dynamics. A causal rational LTI digital filter is BIBO stable when all genuine poles lie strictly inside the unit circle. Analogue-style all-pole low-pass order gives about 6 dB per octave per pole asymptotically; this is not a rule for every digital response.
example: A four-pole low-pass, such as the Moog ladder, falls at about 24 dB per octave.

definition: Sustained oscillation produced by a filter’s feedback without a continuing external audio input. In the ideal linear ladder model, feedback four is the marginal oscillation threshold at the stage corner frequency; real circuit nonlinearities limit practical amplitude.
example: In Stilson and Smith's ladder model, self-oscillation sets in as the feedback k approaches 4.

definition: The formula that says how a digital filter computes each output sample from the current and past inputs and, for recursive filters, past outputs.
example: y[n] = y[n−1] + a × (x[n] − y[n−1]) is the difference equation of a one-pole low-pass.

definition: The values a filter remembers between samples, such as its previous output. State must persist across blocks. Independently filtered voices need separate state; filtering a summed mix once is a deliberate shared-filter design.

A high-pass response obtained here by subtracting a one-pole low-pass output from its input. It rejects a constant input after settling, but its high-frequency gain and corner behaviour depend on the coefficient; it is not automatically a unity-normalised counterpart.

A high-pass filter used to reject a signal’s constant offset after settling, usually with a low corner frequency. It also changes the gain and phase of nearby non-zero frequencies, so choose its response for the audio band you need to preserve.
example: A pulse wave with width 0.3 has a DC offset of −0.4, which a DC blocker removes.

definition: An infinite impulse response filter: its response to one isolated impulse has an indefinitely long tail in exact arithmetic. Recursive feedback implements common IIR designs efficiently. Stable designs decay, while an unstable recursion can grow instead; coefficient and state handling therefore matter.
example: A one-pole low-pass with coefficient a has the impulse response a, a(1 − a), a(1 − a)², and so on.

definition: A general second-order IIR filter section with five coefficients, using the current and two previous inputs and the two previous outputs. With the right coefficients it becomes a low-pass, high-pass, band-pass, notch, peaking or shelving filter.
example: Two cascaded low-pass biquads give a 24 dB/octave slope.

definition: Robert Bristow-Johnson's widely used set of formulas for biquad coefficients (low-pass, high-pass, band-pass, notch, peaking and shelving) from a frequency, Q or bandwidth, and gain. It is now published as a W3C note and uses the bilinear transform with prewarping.
example: For the cookbook low-pass, the gain at the cutoff frequency equals Q.

definition: The textbook ways of wiring a filter's difference equation, straight from its coefficients. Direct forms are efficient for fixed filters but can click or misbehave when their coefficients change quickly, as in a fast cutoff sweep.

A state-variable filter built around a two-integrator loop that can produce low-pass, band-pass and high-pass outputs together. The classic Chamberlin discretisation has cutoff and resonance limits. Trapezoidal versions such as the reviewed Simper/Wishnick structures have stronger modulation-stability behaviour within their positive, finite supported parameter ranges.

Approximating an integral over one sample interval using the average of its endpoint inputs. It leads to the bilinear-transform integrator used in modern state-variable filters. With the appropriate prewarping, parameter range and state structure, such designs can track cutoff accurately and tolerate fast modulation; this is not a guarantee for every filter made with the rule.

A way of implementing an analogue filter's feedback loop digitally without adding a unit delay to the loop, by solving the loop's equation for each sample. It keeps the digital filter's tuning and resonance close to the analogue original.
A delay of exactly one sample. Putting one in a feedback loop is the simplest way to make it computable digitally, but it changes the filter's tuning and resonance behaviour.

Robert Moog's patented filter: four one-pole low-pass stages in series (24 dB per octave) with negative feedback from the output to the input. Raising the feedback adds resonance, reduces the bass, and eventually makes the filter self-oscillate.
example: In Stilson and Smith's model, feedback k = 3 cuts the DC gain to 1/4, about −12 dB.

definition: A mapping from an analogue rational filter to a digital one that maps the stable left half-plane into the digital unit circle. It warps frequency nonlinearly, so prewarping is used to place selected design frequencies accurately. Fixed-setting stability preservation does not by itself prove a time-varying implementation stable.
Adjusting a design frequency before the bilinear transform so that, after the transform's frequency squeeze, the digital filter's cutoff lands exactly where intended.
A filter's gain at each frequency, usually plotted in decibels against a logarithmic frequency axis. Together with the phase response it makes up the frequency response.

A system that obeys superposition and whose response does not change when the input is shifted in time. In steady state an LTI filter changes a sine component’s amplitude and phase without changing its frequency. A filter with coefficients changing during processing is time-varying, so the fixed-response description is insufficient.

The conventional rounded name for a half-power response point, whose amplitude is about 0.7071 of the reference level and whose exact level is about minus 3.0103 decibels. A literal minus 3.000 decibel crossing differs slightly. Resonant designs may define their reference frequency differently.
A filter that boosts or cuts a band around a centre frequency while leaving frequencies far from it unchanged; the standard band of a parametric EQ.
The International Conference on Digital Audio Effects, an annual academic conference where much audio DSP research, including work on time-varying filters, is published.
An audio software company run by Andrew Simper, who published widely used technical papers on stable, modulation-friendly digital filters such as the trapezoidal state-variable filter.
The vowel-like sound of a resonant filter whose cutoff sweeps up and down, as in a guitar wah pedal or a synth filter sweep with high resonance.

Moving a filter’s cutoff over time, by hand, envelope or LFO, so the sound opens up or closes down. An octave-based sweep gives equal frequency ratios per equal control step; other sweep laws are valid too. Smoothing abrupt control updates can reduce zipper noise.
Using the note number as a modulation source, typically to raise the filter cutoff for higher notes so the timbre stays consistent across the keyboard.
example: With 100% key tracking, playing an octave higher also raises the cutoff by an octave.

definition: A table of modulation routes, each with a source, a destination and a signed amount. Each destination adds up its contributions in its own natural unit (octaves for cutoff, semitones for pitch), then converts once and clamps.
example: Routes env → cutoff 3 octaves and LFO → cutoff 0.5 octaves let both move the cutoff at once.

definition: A signal used to vary a sound parameter, such as an LFO, envelope, note velocity, key tracking or performance controller. Its ownership is a design choice: note envelopes and velocities are commonly per voice; an explicitly shared LFO or a conventional MIDI-channel controller can steer several voices together.
A parameter that modulation can change, such as pitch, filter cutoff, resonance, gain or pulse width.
How far a modulation source moves its destination, ideally in the destination's musical unit: cents or semitones for pitch, octaves for cutoff, a fraction or decibels for gain.
example: A vibrato depth of ±50 cents swings a 440 Hz note between about 427 and 453 Hz.

definition: A modulation source that runs one way only, from 0 to +1, so it moves its destination in one direction from the set value, as a tremolo that only reduces volume or an envelope that only opens the filter. A bipolar value b (−1 to +1) converts to unipolar with (b + 1) / 2.
example: A bipolar LFO value of −0.5 becomes a unipolar 0.25.

definition: In this synth context, a stepped random LFO that chooses a new random value at a trigger or cycle boundary and holds it until the next update. Abrupt level changes can click when mapped to gain, so a short slew can preserve the stepped character while reducing transients. This is a modulation use, distinct from an ADC’s sample-and-hold circuit.
Resetting an LFO's phase at each note-on so every note starts its wobble the same way. Without it, a free-running LFO is at a different point in its cycle for each note.

Deriving an LFO rate from song tempo and a chosen musical note length, so its cycle duration follows the beat. Aligning the cycle’s phase with a transport beat additionally needs a suitable phase/reset policy.
example: At 120 BPM, one LFO cycle per quarter note is 2 Hz.

definition: A note lasting half a beat in common time (half a quarter note), called a quaver in British usage.
example: When the tempo beat is a quarter note, 90 BPM makes an eighth note last one third of a second, so one LFO cycle per eighth is 3 Hz.

definition: Frequency modulation applied through exponential musical-pitch units, such as octaves or semitones. A zero-mean sine in octave units gives asymmetric upward and downward hertz changes and raises the arithmetic mean instantaneous frequency. That arithmetic mean is distinct from the pitch perceived from the resulting spectrum.
example: A ±1-octave exponential swing around 440 Hz goes up 440 Hz but down only 220 Hz; the average is about 494.5 Hz.

definition: Modulation that adds a frequency deviation proportional to its source in hertz. A zero-mean source preserves the mean instantaneous frequency in the ideal model. This does not guarantee perceived pitch, prevent aliasing, or make an implementation with clipped negative frequencies equivalent.

Controlling how quickly a parameter moves between values so abrupt targets become short transitions. A bounded-slope ramp is a literal slew limiter; a one-pole smoother rounds steps exponentially rather than imposing the same fixed slope limit. Either can soften stepped-LFO gain changes.

The part of a polyphonic synth that decides which voice from its fixed pool plays each new note: a free voice if there is one, otherwise one chosen to steal, such as the oldest note, the quietest voice or one already releasing.
example: With two voices busy on notes 60 and 64, an allocator that steals the oldest gives note 67 the voice that was playing 60.

definition: A circuit or process that multiplies a signal by a gain, usually making it bigger. In a synth voice the amplifier (often a VCA) is driven by the amplitude envelope so notes start and stop, and digitally it is a single multiplication per sample; a power amplifier is the kind that drives loudspeakers.
example: A gain of 0.5 halves the amplitude, which is about −6 dB.

definition: An effect that mixes a signal with slightly delayed, slowly pitch-wobbling copies of itself, making one sound seem like several playing together. Sweeping a pulse wave's width gives a similar shimmering movement.

A delay that is not a whole number of samples, made by interpolating between neighbouring samples (for example with linear interpolation or an allpass filter). Physical models such as Karplus–Strong need one to tune a delay-line loop exactly, because a whole-sample loop length only gives certain pitches.
example: At 48 kHz, one 220 Hz period is about 218.18 samples in total. With a half-sample averaging-filter delay, the remaining delay-line/interpolation path needs about 217.68 samples; count all loop delays when tuning.

definition: A filter whose coefficients change while it runs, as when a synth's cutoff is swept by an envelope or LFO. Changing coefficients can cause clicks, and a feedback (IIR) filter can even become unstable although every individual coefficient setting is stable, so some filter structures cope with modulation far better than others.

The dimensionless fraction of one oscillator cycle spent at the high level. Some synth controls call this pulse width; distinguish it from a pulse duration in seconds. A half-cycle high interval gives an equal-duty square wave.
example: A duty fraction of 0.25 spends one quarter of each cycle high. At 100 Hz that is 2.5 ms; at 200 Hz it is 1.25 ms.

definition: Changing a pulse oscillator’s duty fraction over time to change its harmonic pattern. This changes the audio waveform itself; it is different from using a high-frequency PWM carrier to encode an average control voltage.

Keeping only finitely many terms of an ideal Fourier series. A strict harmonic cutoff limits bandwidth but creates ripple near a jump. This operation differs from truncating a numeric value towards zero.

Bounded-input bounded-output stability: every input with a finite amplitude bound produces an output with a finite amplitude bound. Fixed finite-length FIR filters with finite coefficients satisfy it; a causal rational IIR requires its genuine poles inside the unit circle.

The average value of an analysis window, used to correct coherent sinusoidal amplitude measurements after windowing. Windowing changes both peak width and amplitude; multiplying every bin by twice the reciprocal of the sample count alone does not correct the window’s gain.
The reference corner of an individual filter stage. Cascading stages and adding feedback changes the combined response, so the stage corner need not equal the final filter’s half-power cutoff.

The family of mathematical functions that gives sinusoidal FM/PM carrier and sideband amplitudes as a function of modulation index. Particular indices make individual components zero; increasing index does not simply increase every sideband monotonically.

Signal content distributed over a wide range of frequencies. A short abrupt waveform change can have broad spectral content, but whether it is audible as a click also depends on amplitude, duration and masking.

A listening condition in which one sound makes another harder to hear. The audibility of an alias or click depends on nearby spectral content, relative levels and the listener; a relative decibel value alone is not an audibility threshold.

The initial envelope stage after a trigger, rising from its current level towards the attack peak. Its control can specify a stage duration or a time constant, depending on the implementation; define that convention rather than assuming the knob equals the completed rise time.

The envelope stage started when the gate turns off, reducing its current value towards the idle level. An exponential implementation approaches zero indefinitely in exact arithmetic, so a practical voice needs a documented stopping threshold or finite end rule.

The highest relevant delay or derivative order of a rational filter model after cancellations. For the analogue-style all-pole low-pass examples it corresponds to the number of poles. Zeros and digital frequency mapping mean pole count alone is not a universal decibel-per-octave rule.

A short waveform or coefficient sequence added around a known waveform edge to approximate the desired low-pass-smoothed transition. BLEP methods align these contributions to the edge’s fractional-sample position. Longer or differently shaped kernels trade cost, delay and spectral error.

A component that stores energy in an electric field between conductors separated by an insulator. For ideal fixed capacitance, current flows when its voltage changes; a constant voltage can remain across it with zero steady current. Capacitors in RC circuits charge or discharge over time and are used in filtering, coupling and envelope generators.
example: Charging a capacitor through a resistor from a DC supply produces an exponential voltage rise.
